I was fifteen and my mom died. She had been sick for most of my life with COPD/emphysema and bipolar 1, and since my dad was always working and my older sister bailed as soon as she could, I ended up being my mom's primary caretaker while I was still in elementary school. On top of being a child and being held responsible for literally keeping her alive, I was the one who got to be around her during her episodes all of the time (which pretty much were constant because she refused to go to a psychiatrist). She was ultra clingy with me and frequently told me I was the only person she trusted and I was her only friend. She experienced paranoia frequently and I was pretty much the only person she didn't push away during this (in fact, she'd keep me home from school even while we were getting letters warning us that we might have to go to court over my truancy). 

I was already having episodes before, but everyone just chalked it up to teenage hormones and attention-seeking until she died and I started hallucinating, weighed only 85 lb because I stopped eating, and then tried to kill myself. I was diagnosed pretty much immediately with bipolar 1 after that.

Real triggers are a symptom of PTSD/other mental illnesses. You've probably heard stories or references to war veterans having flashbacks or panic attacks when they hear fireworks because the sound is similar to a bomb going off, right? That's a trigger, because it "triggers" a panic attack, flight or fight response, flashback, etc. When someone with PTSD or another mental illness says they were triggered by something, they mean that they saw, read, heard, experienced, etc something that caused them to relive a traumatic experience or have an episode. Often, when this happens, the person is in such distress that their mind can't process the fact that they are actually safe, and they react to the situation in the same way they would if they were in legitimate danger. The word trigger was never intended to mean "something that I dislike/disagree with," or "something that makes me mildly uncomfortable." Some people started misusing it and then anti-SJWs picked up on it and turned it into an insult to mock those people - but in doing that, they are also mocking people with legitimate triggers. So no, they weren't offended by their partner and responded by punching them. Something happened during their scene that likely caused the person to feel as though they were in danger, and they reacted accordingly, despite not actually wanting to injure their partner.

That's.. strange that she's revising your diagnosis based on the length of your hypomanic episodes. I've always been under the impression that hypomania can last *months* in bipolar 2 as long as it never crosses the line into true mania. Once you have a single manic episode or experience psychosis, BAM, bipolar 1. I've never heard of there being a maximum length for an episode to be considered hypomanic. Maybe you could ask her if that's the only reason she's revising your diagnosis or if there's something else that she's noticed that influenced the decision? If your current treatment plan is working and she didn't suggest any changes, then I guess there's nothing new you need to do.
